items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: The interviewee mentions 'Cannon' in the context of radio shows ('Horace and Cannon and Blakey') and as a member of specific groups ('Miles sextet with Cannon and Trane', 'Nat, Cannon, Yusef, Zawinul, Sam Jones and Louis Hayes'), praising his skills ('Cannon knew how to work an audience. He was bril

ctx.x: Okay. So what do you say to him as far as the tunes? You say Fathead, what do you got here that —

Well it varies from artist to artist. With David, he was open to me suggesting songs and he also listened to the radio so he didn’t just listen to jazz. So he was open. And when I started saying I don’t want to work with like jazz rhythm sections, I want to work with R&B studio cats like Bernard Purdie and Richard Tee and Eric Gale and Chuck Rainey. I want to work with those guys. But they had a very high level of musicianship beyond just, you know, playing on commercial records. The guys could play. So when they…

that. And also jazz radio at that time, listen I played Lady and Trane and Miles and Prez and you know like Ellington and Mingus, all that stuff. But the thrust of my show was the popular jazz of the day: Horace and Cannon and Blakey and you know, whoever had like a jazz hit or whoever had albums that went beyond the three, four, five thousand selling jazz records.

items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I noticed that when I was listening to the Cannonball thing you sent, “Radio Nights.” ... [INTERVIEWEE] It was — all his live records except for two of them were made in the studio with an audience.

ctx.x: is too long a story to bore you with but through a friend, Bernie Dreighton, I found some tapes he had made at a small club in Brooklyn in the sixties: Blakey, Kenny Dorham, you know, people like that, guys who’d play these small clubs in Brooklyn to work out material before they recorded for Blue Note or Prestige or stuff like that. So in trying to clear those, I came across other collections. At a certain point we had isolated a quarter of a million hours of privately — in lieu of the word illegally — recorded…
I noticed that when I was listening to the Cannonball thing you sent, “Radio Nights.” I’m listening to him and I’ve not heard that kind of playing on even his best records. It was somehow—
It was — all his live records except for two of them were made in the studio with an audience.
